video_title: The Next Evolution of Trend Following ft. Nick Baltas | Systematic Investor | Ep.410
gist: Nick Baltas (Goldman Sachs) and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen review a recovering July 2026 for CTAs driven by a rates sell-off and commodities, then work through four research papers: Graham Capital on how added markets stop paying above ~70-80 unless they are exotic commodities, One River on the first/second responder hedging stack, and two papers arguing thematics and 'narrative momentum' should be treated as missing risk factors and as the upstream engine of price momentum. Baltas's core argument is that themes are just a tagging/dimensionality-reduction exercise, but one that biases risk models upward if ignored and that explains where trends come from before they show up in price.

themes.theme: AI model churn and the human-in-the-loop constraint

insights.claim: The frontier 'best' AI model is now being displaced roughly every 10 to 19 days versus three to four months last year, which makes AI tooling integration a moving target for large financial institutions rather than a one-off procurement decision.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Vendor lock-in and model-specific engineering are depreciating assets; firms building on a single model provider face repeated re-integration costs, and the churn favors abstraction layers over deep single-model tuning.
insights.quote: the quote unquote best model at the moment get replaced like every 10 I think it was every 10 days or every 19 days

insights.claim: For individual users the marginal value of upgrading to the newest AI model is close to zero because the current best model becomes the default a month later, so staying one version behind costs little.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Argues against paying premium pricing for frontier access at the individual/desk level, and implies consumer AI subscription pricing power is weaker than the release cadence suggests.
insights.quote: you might as well just use the version I don't know t minus one. You probably get pretty much all you need without even having to to upgrade to the latest model

insights.claim: LLM hallucination in finance research has shifted from obviously fabricated names and papers a year ago to plausible-but-wrong answers on open-ended questions, which is a more dangerous failure mode because it is undetectable without domain expertise.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The bottleneck for AI in investment research is verification capacity, not generation capacity; firms without senior domain experts to audit output carry unpriced model risk.
insights.quote: had I not known what the performance has been I would have like okay that sounds reasonable it was dead wrong

insights.claim: AI at a large investment bank is currently deployed mainly to accelerate research, information collection, synthesis and coding rather than to generate investment decisions, with human-in-the-loop supervision mandated partly by regulation.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for AI-driven margin gains at banks: efficiency in the research stack, not headcount-free autonomous decisioning, at least while supervision requirements bind.

insights.claim: Machine learning and AI methods have become the overarching theme across essentially every topic at a quant research conference, spanning portfolio construction, equity forecasting, sentiment and thematic association, without being a scheduled agenda item.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Signals that the academic-to-practitioner pipeline for systematic strategies is now ML-native, which raises the bar for what counts as differentiated quant research.
insights.quote: the use of the machine learning and AI models has become now you know very very common um in pretty much all the topics we had

themes.theme: July 2026 CTA turnaround and its drivers

insights.claim: After a weak June and a soft start to July, CTAs turned positive in late July led by energies, currencies and fixed income, but with uneven participation across markets within each sector rather than broad sector-wide trends.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: A 'trend pickers' market rewards breadth and market-selection dispersion, so manager return dispersion within the CTA peer group should be wider than usual this month.

insights.claim: The July gain in trend programs was primarily driven by the sell-off in rates and the resulting short fixed-income exposures, with commodities contributing both month-to-date and year-to-date while equities and FX were flat to slightly down.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Current CTA P&L is levered to the short-rates trade continuing; a sharp bond rally is the main near-term drawdown risk for the strategy.
insights.quote: this is primarily driven by rates activity in the last week really. Uh so the sell off in the rates and obviously the short exposures has been helping quite substantially

insights.claim: Trend models that impose a threshold suppressing position size on weak signals lagged in July, because the small short rates positions taken on weak signals turned out to be the profitable ones.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Signal-response shape (linear vs. thresholded) is a live driver of manager dispersion right now; thresholded programs give up convexity to weak-signal luck in fast regime turns.

insights.claim: As of mid-July 2026 the reported index levels were: BTOP50 +1.34% MTD and +10% YTD, SG CTA index +0.89% MTD and +10.37% YTD, SG Trend index +0.94% MTD and +10.15% YTD, short-term traders index -0.6% MTD and +4.52% YTD, MSCI World -0.84% MTD and +9% YTD, and the US aggregate bond index -0.96% MTD and -0.12% YTD.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Trend following is beating both equities and bonds year to date in 2026, strengthening the diversification pitch to allocators at a time when bonds are flat to negative.

insights.claim: Short-term trading programs are badly lagging medium-term trend in 2026, up only about 4.5% year to date versus roughly 10% for the main trend indices.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case against paying up for faster trend as a hedge; allocators sizing speed exposure should note the persistent medium-term premium.

insights.claim: The 2026 March V-shape was a fast recovery rather than the usual fast drop followed by a slower reversion, which made it less damaging to trend followers than the equivalent V-shapes of prior years.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The recurring roughly one-per-year V-shape remains the main structural tax on trend, but its shape matters as much as its existence when forecasting CTA drawdowns.

insights.claim: Dynamic volatility scaling was the specific model enhancement that paid off through the 2026 March episode, validating research work done in advance rather than any market call.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Vol-targeting mechanics, not signal changes, were the differentiator in the year's sharpest reversal; a diligence question worth asking any trend manager about 2026 attribution.
insights.quote: some of the work that we have put into thinking about dynamic volatility scaling actually played out quite nicely

insights.claim: Carry has been a very strong diversifier to trend in 2026 across both FX and commodities, with commodity carry helped by backwardation tied to geopolitical activity.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Multi-strategy trend-plus-carry sleeves are compounding better than pure trend this year; the commodity carry leg is exposed to any normalization of the curve if geopolitical risk premium fades.
insights.quote: it's also been a very good year for diversifiers to to trend following

insights.claim: Skew-driven reversion strategies had a strong first four to five months of 2026 but have themselves been mean-reverting since, while the aggregate of trend plus reversion still nets positive in months where trend leads.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Supports the multi-strat packaging pitch: the combination is smoother than either sleeve, which is the actual product being sold to allocators.

insights.claim: Investor interest in trend and defensive systematic strategies is rising across all fronts, driven by recent performance and by institutions increasingly focused on protecting the downside.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Flows into trend tend to be performance-chasing; a run of strong months plus a defensive narrative is the classic setup for asset gathering and eventual capacity pressure.

themes.theme: How many markets a trend follower should trade

insights.claim: Graham Capital's 'An Expanding Market Universe' paper finds that once a trend program crosses roughly 70 to 80 markets, adding progressively less liquid markets adds little incremental performance.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for evaluating managers who market 300-market universes as an edge; breadth claims above ~80 markets need to be justified by market type, not count.
insights.quote: as soon as you cross 70 to 80 markets, the less liquid markets do not really add much in terms of performance

insights.claim: The breadth result is conditional on market type: adding illiquid macro markets such as EM equities, minor currencies or interest rate swaps adds nothing because the principal components are already spanned, whereas exotic and Chinese commodities do add incremental long-term value beyond 100 markets.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The only breadth worth paying for is genuinely new dimensionality, which today means exotic and Chinese commodity markets; treat added macro markets as capacity dilution rather than alpha.

insights.claim: Because a top-down risk budget fixes each sector's total risk contribution, adding more markets within an existing sector simply divides the same risk across more instruments at worse liquidity, degrading program capacity without adding return.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Explains why universe expansion can be actively harmful: it converts liquid capacity into illiquid capacity at constant expected return, raising execution and crowding risk.

insights.claim: Baltas's programs typically operate between 50 and 100 markets, which he says coincides with sitting around the 20-parameter bucket in how they think about the world.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A named practitioner anchor for universe size at a major bank, useful as a comparison point when diligencing CTA breadth claims.
insights.quote: we typically operate between the 50 and the 100

insights.claim: Universe size should be set by objective: a small core universe maximizes crisis alpha because principal components like equity beta and duration dominate in downturns, while a broader universe favors long-term return at the expense of defensiveness.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Allocators buying trend as a hedge should prefer concentrated core-market programs; those buying it as a return engine should prefer broad ones. Mixing the two objectives in one mandate guarantees disappointment.
insights.quote: if the focus is to have more crisis alpha or defensiveness, you should focus on a small core universe because in a downturn, the principal components dominate

insights.claim: The expected performance gain from adding markets is not linear because lower liquidity introduces a drag, so backtested breadth benefits overstate realized ones.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Discount breadth-driven backtest improvements by an execution-cost haircut, particularly for programs marketing exotic-market expansion at scale.

themes.theme: Defensive stacks, leverage and portable alpha

insights.claim: One River Capital's 'The Perfect Hedge' paper by Patrick Castley decomposes a defensive solution into three buckets: option and volatility-based first responders with low basis but high cost, trend following as the second responder, and a third non-responding diversifier that moderates the cost of carry of the first two.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A ready-made template for building a hedging sleeve: pay for convexity only for the flash-crash window, use trend for the multi-month drawdown, and fund both with a flat-to-negative-correlation carry sleeve.

insights.claim: Trend following protects against multi-month crises, not few-day crises, so it is structurally the wrong instrument for flash corrections that option-based hedges are designed to catch.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Investors who judge trend by its behavior in one-week equity shocks are measuring the wrong horizon; the mandate should be benchmarked over quarters.
insights.quote: It's the crisis alpha but not the few day crisis but more like the multimonth crisis

insights.claim: The funding sleeve inside a defensive portfolio must not be a short gamma exposure, because financing a hedge by selling downside risk elsewhere turns the package from a defensive overlay into a relative value trade.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A specific diligence red flag: any 'improved' tail hedge whose long-run performance comes from carry-selling has reintroduced the risk it was hired to remove.
insights.quote: what you end up doing is that you're almost recreating some downside risk from your diversifying entity to finance your hedge. And by all means there's nothing wrong with that. But this is not anymore a defensive overlay.

insights.claim: Making the trend sleeve faster to improve hedging responsiveness is a false economy: it may help for a few days but costs more over the long run, and short-term trend has become worse over the last decade.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Argues against the intuitive allocator move of shortening trend speed for defensiveness; slower is counterintuitively the better long-run hedge.
insights.quote: it might be better for a few days, but it end up costing you more in the long run

insights.claim: When stacking trend on top of an equity-only portfolio, the trend program should be designed with reduced upside equity participation so the investor does not double up on equity risk on the way up.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A concrete design spec for portable alpha mandates: asymmetric equity exposure in the overlay is what makes the leverage safe, not the leverage ratio itself.
insights.quote: I think it should come from the perspective of perhaps reduced upside participation in the trend program. So you don't by design double up on your equities risk on the upside.

insights.claim: For an equity-bond portfolio the worst-case scenario is not falling equities but equities and bonds falling together, which historically coincides with inflation shocks that unfold over a quarter or more.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Defines the hedge that 60/40 investors actually need: protection against correlated inflation-driven drawdowns, which is exactly the multi-month trend-follower window, not equity puts.
insights.quote: The equity bond portfolio is not facing its worst challenge when equities are falling. It is when both are falling. And that is historically associated with inflation shocks.

insights.claim: The objection to leverage in portable alpha is misdirected: the risk is not added notional leverage per se but added leverage on the asset an investor is already highly concentrated in.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A reframing that unlocks stacked-exposure allocations for leverage-averse institutions: measure concentration risk, not gross notional.
insights.quote: it's not that the increased leverage is creating the concern here it's the increased leverage on the asset that you're highly concentrated

insights.claim: Portable alpha and unfunded or stacked exposures have become popular again after a 15 to 20 year absence, with trend following one of the primary vehicles being used inside those structures.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Structural demand tailwind for trend capacity independent of performance; watch for capacity and crowding effects if stacked products keep scaling.

insights.claim: Themes are nothing more than a tagging operation, a categorical grouping of assets sharing a common feature, and are conceptually no different from grouping stocks by the first letter of their name.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Deflates the thematic-product marketing narrative while identifying the one thing that does matter: whether investors actually allocate by the tag, which is what makes the tag economically real.
insights.quote: themes are nothing more than a tagging operation. It's just a categorical way of combining assets in a particular group that share some common feature

insights.claim: Risk factors are not the same as risk premia: countries are a significant component of a risk model but carry no systematic compensation, and the same distinction applies to thematics, which can explain risk without offering a premium.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Guards against the common product error of selling a thematic exposure as a harvestable premium when it is only a risk-explanation dimension.
insights.quote: Risk factors are not always risk premier. risk factors explain risk.

insights.claim: The paper 'Thematic Investing as Missing Factors' by Wai Lee shows that failing to include thematics in a covariance matrix biases predicted portfolio risk upward, meaning portfolios are riskier than measured and risk is being distributed inaccurately.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Direct implication for risk-parity and vol-targeted books: thematic clustering means realized risk exceeds model risk, so nominal vol targets are being breached in thematically concentrated regimes.
insights.quote: if we don't account for those then our prediction of portfolio risk is biased downwards sorry it's biased upwards so we're more risky than what we should have been had we accounted for it

insights.claim: Thematic clustering is short-lived and point-in-time, so covariance matrices built purely on historical correlations systematically miss the clusters that matter tomorrow, including cross-asset clusters linking specific equity regions, currencies and commodities to a single macro shock.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The actionable extension is applying thematic overlays to multi-asset trend covariance estimation, not just stock selection, to avoid unknowingly concentrating risk in one macro narrative.

insights.claim: Thematic correlation is now amplified beyond sector effects because investors literally think and allocate in packages, as with memory chips where sector membership and the AI narrative reinforce each other.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Cross-correlations inside hot themes will keep rising with allocation flows, shrinking the diversification benefit of holding multiple names in the same narrative.

insights.claim: Systematic investing profits from only two sources: compensated risk sharing where an investor is paid to hold what others do not want, and behavioral or structural inefficiencies such as leverage-constrained pension funds bidding up high-beta names and creating the low-beta anomaly.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A test to apply to any new systematic strategy pitch, including thematics: if it maps to neither pillar, the backtest is probably data mining.

themes.theme: Narrative momentum as the engine behind price momentum

insights.claim: Narrative-driven allocation creates the price pressure that later shows up as price momentum: an asset becomes hyped, allocation follows, an inelastic market establishes a price path, and short-term momentum signals then capture it.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: If narrative flow is the upstream cause, measuring it gives an earlier entry than price-based trend signals, which is the actual edge claim behind narrative momentum.
insights.quote: Something becomes very hypy. And because it's hypy, there is more allocation to it. And because there's more allocation to it, some price path is started being established.

insights.claim: The 'narrative momentum' paper finds that stocks with high exposure to narratives gaining popularity outperform stocks exposed to fading narratives, which is distinct from repackaged price momentum because it identifies the demand engine that precedes the price move.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A potential signal overlay for equity and multi-asset allocation models: scale exposure up when an asset's narrative score is rising, not just when its price trend is positive.
insights.quote: the stocks that happen to have higher exposure on naratives that are becoming more popular

insights.claim: The narrative momentum research is built on a point-in-time dataset of roughly 13.3 million articles, filings, blogs and news agency items running from around 2012-2014 forward, with robustness checks using alternative narrative definitions including 57 JEL-classification-driven categories.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The dataset's point-in-time construction is the paper's real asset and the main barrier to replication; the short sample from 2012 onward is the corresponding weakness.

insights.claim: Backtesting narratives faces a look-ahead problem analogous to the factor zoo: a 'narrative zoo' of overlapping, highly correlated topics where narratives only become testable after they become known.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Treat narrative backtests with the same skepticism applied to newly discovered equity factors; correlation clusters mean apparent breadth overstates independent evidence.
insights.quote: So I think here we have like a narrative zoo

insights.claim: The look-ahead objection is defensible because narratives are correlated: a persistent healthcare narrative would have captured COVID without needing to know COVID in advance, just as book-to-price and earnings-to-price both proxy valuation.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: The practical design rule is to use a small set of evergreen topics rather than chasing named themes, which is what makes narrative signals implementable out of sample.
insights.quote: Nobody knew the straits of horm but people did know geopolitical tensions. So I would expect the two to move together.

insights.claim: A workable narrative universe should be roughly 30 to 60 evergreen topics such as trade wars, stagflation, capital expenditure or ESG, not 500, because overly prescriptive narratives just produce five different labels for the same underlying event.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: A concrete specification for anyone building a narrative overlay: dimensionality-reduce to a few dozen persistent topics rather than tracking every trending theme.
insights.quote: We cannot have 500 of them. Possibly like 30 or 40 are enough.

insights.claim: There is no reason a narrative such as stagflation should outperform over the long run, so thematics offer timing-driven and risk-explanation value rather than a harvestable risk premium.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Positions thematic signals as a dynamic allocation tool with decay, meaning they must be traded and rebalanced rather than held as a strategic allocation.

insights.claim: Price is not necessarily the best predictor of the underlying price process, only the most easily observable and empirically validated one, and macro regime, price path and thematic exposure are complementary transformations of the same latent signal.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Frames the next evolution of trend following as multi-proxy signal blending, price plus economic trends plus narrative strength, rather than replacing price signals.
insights.quote: the price path in itself is not necessarily the best predictor but it's an easily observable easily calculated and empirically validated

insights.claim: The rise of thematic frameworks is a response to limited investor attention and excess dimensionality, and its value is largely in making decisions tractable for discretionary human investors rather than for systematic processes.
insights.speaker: Nick Baltas
insights.so_what: Implies thematic products are as much a distribution and cognition innovation as an alpha source, which tempers expectations for their standalone returns.

insights.claim: The skeptical case is that thematic grouping is largely Wall Street repackaging what sector classification has done for decades, since simply grouping healthcare companies together captures most of the same commonality without any narrative machinery.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for thematic products: they must demonstrate incremental explanatory power over plain sector classifications before justifying higher fees.
